L62: # SABER: Uncovering Vulnerabilities in Safety Alignment via Cross-Layer Residual Connection
L63: 
L64: Maithili Joshi ^{†}^{†}thanks: Equal contribution.    Palash Nandi^{1}^{1}footnotemark: 1    Tanmoy Chakraborty Affiliation: Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, India Affiliation: maithilij2003@gmail.com, {eez228472, tanchak}@iitd.ac.in
L65: ###### Abstract
L66: Large Language Models (LLMs) with safe-alignment training are powerful instruments with robust language comprehension capabilities. These models typically undergo meticulous alignment procedures involving human feedback to ensure the acceptance of safe inputs while rejecting harmful or unsafe ones.
L67: However, despite their massive scale and alignment efforts, LLMs remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, where malicious users manipulate the model to produce harmful outputs that it was explicitly trained to avoid. In this study, we find that the safety mechanisms in LLMs are predominantly embedded in the middle-to-late layers.
L68: Building on this insight, we introduce a novel white-box jailbreak method, SABER (S afety A lignment B ypass via E xtra R esiduals), which connects two intermediate layers $s$ and $e$ such that $s<e$, through a residual connection. Our approach achieves a $51\%$ improvement over the best-performing baseline on the HarmBench test set. Furthermore, SABER induces only a marginal shift in perplexity when evaluated on the HarmBench validation set.
L69: The source code is publicly available^{1}^{1} 1 cite50†https://github.com/PalGitts/SABER†github.com .
L70: Warning: This paper contains potentially harmful and offensive content.
L71: ## 1 Introduction
L72: In recent times, safety-aligned Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained widespread popularity for a variety of tasks in professional and social domains cite51†Luo et al. (2022) ; cite52†Tinn et al. (2023) . However, the widespread adoption has exposed exploitable vulnerabilities of LLMs with significant adverse implications cite53†Bengio et al. (2024) . A range of counter mechanisms have been developed from supervised fine-tuning cite54†Ouyang et al. (2022) ; cite55†Bianchi et al.
L73: (2023) , adversarial training cite56†Ganguli et al. (2022) to reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) cite57†Christiano et al. (2017) in order to address the issue. These counter-measurements are formulated to effectively reject malicious queries and ensure that the generated outputs are aligned with human ethical standards.
L74: Complementarily, malicious actors always attempt to identify the gaps or blind spots in the model’s architecture, training data, or training process to evade the established safety-measurements. Traditional approaches generally fall into two categories: (i) white-box, and (ii) black-box. In white-box approaches, the models permit access to internal parts, allowing unethical exploitation of gradients, logits, architectural components cite58†Shayegani et al. (2023) .
L75: In contrast, jailbreaking approaches are limited to template completion, prompt rewriting, and prompt perturbation for black-box based methods cite59†Yi et al. (2024) ; cite60†Xu et al. (2024) ; cite61†Jin et al. (2024) .
L76: Recently, there is a notable progress in the use of activation steering techniques cite62†Zou et al. (2023a) ; cite63†Turner et al. (2023) ; cite64†Panickssery et al. () and mechanistic interpretability cite65†Bricken et al. () ; cite66†Marks et al. (2024) ; cite67†Nanda et al. (2023) ; cite68†Templeton et al. (2024) . cite69†Arditi et al.
L77: (2024) argued that the refusal in LLMS are mediated by a one-dimensional subspace and proposed a novel white-box jailbreak method that disables refusal behavior of LLMs but retains other capabilities. Sourcing inspiration from it, we introduce SABER, a novel approach that leverages cross-layer residual connection to circumvent the safety alignment of LLMs.
L78: First, we analyze representational divergence between harmful and benign inputs to identify boundaries where safety alignment mechanisms are most active; next, we determine an optimal scaling factor that preserves language capabilities; and finally, we select two specific layers, s and e, where the intervention is most effective. SABER attempts to override the safety alignment by drawing a residual connection from $s$ to $e$. We apply SABER on four different models and compare against six baseline methods.
L79: Our approach shows up to a $51\%$ improvement over the best performing baseline. This substantial gain indicates the effectiveness of our method SABER.
L80: ## 2 Related Work
L81: The taxonomy of jailbreak attacks is primarily classified into two main classes: white-box and black-box cite59†Yi et al. (2024) , based on the transparency of the target language model to the attacker. In a white-box attack, the malicious user can access to the LLM’s architecture, training data, and algorithms. It allows them to extract critical information from the gradients cite70†Zou et al. (2023b) , logits cite71†Zhang et al. (2023) , or alter the internal architecture cite72†Ball et al.
L82: (2024) to influence the model’s behavior. cite73†Qi et al. (2023) demonstrated that fine-tuning LLMs with just a few adversarial instances can dismantle the safety-alignment. A similar phenomenon has also been reported in other research works cite74†Yang et al. (2023) ; cite75†Zhan et al. (2023) . cite76†Zhao et al.
L83: (2023) demonstrated how LLMs learn and forget unsafe examples during fine-tuning or the importance of accurate detection of incorrect or misleading information, as it enables their exclusion from the training data, thereby improving the reliability and robustness of the resulting models cite77†Barrón-Cedeño et al. (2024) . Studies indicate the prevalence of explicit or implicit toxic content in memes cite78†Sharma et al. (2022a) ; cite79†Sharma et al. (2022b) ; cite80†Sharma et al. (2023) ; cite81†Nandi et al.
L84: (2024) , underscoring their potential averse impacts. The backdoor attack cite82†Bai et al. (2024) ; cite83†Bansal et al. (2023) introduced by cite84†Wang et al. (2025) bypasses the existing meme hate-detection frameworks.
L85: The black-box attacks are limited to template completion, prompt rewriting, and perturbation due to lack of access to model internals. cite85†Li et al. (2023) generated nested scenarios based on the personification ability of LLMs, while cite86†Ding et al. (2023) utilized both scenario nesting and prompt rewriting. cite87†Wei et al. (2023) exploited in-context learning to subvert safety alignment using adversarial examples, later extended by merging the principle of GCG cite70†Zou et al.
L86: (2023b) with in-context attacks cite88†Wang et al. (2023) .
L87: Unlike existing jailbreaking approaches that require fine-tuning to craft specific adversarial prompts, our method operates directly on the model’s forward pass without any training overhead. Recently, cite69†Arditi et al. (2024) showed that LLM refusals operate in a one-dimensional subspace and proposed using a difference-in-means vector between benign and toxic prompts to disable refusal behavior while preserving other capabilities.
L88: In contrast, our proposed SABER method identifies two distinct layers: a source layer $s$ and a target layer $e$, with weaker and stronger understanding of the safety alignment, respectively. The residual connection between them allows information to circumvent safety enforcing transformations by routing normalized activations from layer $s$ directly to layer $e$ with a calibrated scaling factor $\lambda$.
L89: ## 3 Dataset
L90: In this section, we outline the details of the datasets utilized in our research. We use separate datasets for benign and toxic inputs for evaluation. For toxic inputs, we use HarmBench cite89†Mazeika et al. (2024) that contains four categories: standard behaviors (direct harmful queries), copyright-related behaviors, contextual behaviors, and multimodal behaviors.
L91: We focus exclusively on the standard behaviour category, split between $41$ instances for validation ($\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}}^{\text{ val}}$) and 159 instances for test ($\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}}^{\text{ test}}$). In addition, we sample 41 benign prompts for validation ($\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}^{\text{ val}}$) from the ALPACA dataset cite90†Taori et al. (2023) , ensuring balance with $\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}}^{\text{ val}}$.
L92: ## 4 Proposed Methodology
L93: ### 4.1 Background
L94: An autoregressive decoder-only transformer $\mathcal{M}_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}$ is optimized to predict the next token by maximizing the likelihood of it over the vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$ conditioned on the previous tokens. It maps the input sequence $x=[x_{1}\cdots x_{M}]\in\mathcal{X},x_{i}\in\mathcal{V}$ to a probability distribution $y\in\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}$.
L95: The model consists of $L$ layers of transformer blocks, where the hidden state $h_{i}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is the output of layer $l$ for token $i$. The initial hidden state for each token is computed as the sum of token embedding and positional encoding, i.e., $h_{i}^{(0)}=\texttt{EMB}(x_{i})+\texttt{PE}(x_{i})$, where $\texttt{EMB}(x_{i})$ provides the token embedding and $\texttt{PE}(x_{i})$ returns the corresponding positional encoding.
L96: Thereafter, for each layer $l$, the hidden states are updated through the following sequence of computations:
L97:  |  | $\displaystyle\tilde{h}_{i}^{(l-1)}=\texttt{LNORM}(h_{i}^{(l-1)})$  |  | (1)
L98:  |  | $\displaystyle h_{i}^{(l,\text{ mid})}=h_{i}^{(l-1)}+\texttt{MHAttn}^{(l)}(\tilde{h}^{(l-1)}_{1:i})$  |
L99:  |  | $\displaystyle\tilde{h}_{i}^{(l,\text{ mid})}=\texttt{LNORM}(h_{i}^{(l,\text{ mid})})$  |
L100:  |  | $\displaystyle h_{i}^{(l)}=h_{i}^{(l,\text{ mid})}+\texttt{MLP}^{(l)}(\tilde{h}_{i}^{(l,\text{ mid})})$  |
L101: Here, the input to each layer $l$ is denoted by $h_{i}^{(l-1)}$ and normalized using layer normalization (LNORM). While the operation $\texttt{MHAttn}^{(l)}$ refers to the masked multi-head self-attention, the position-wise feedforward network is represented by $\texttt{MLP}^{(l)}$. In general, $\texttt{MHAttn}^{(l)}$ operates on the normalized hidden states $\tilde{h}_{1:i}^{(l-1)}$ obtained by normalizing the output of the previous layer ${h}_{i}^{(l-1)}$.
L102: In contrast, $\texttt{MLP}^{(l)}$ operates on the normalized output of the attention-residual combination $\tilde{h}_{i}^{(l,\text{ mid})}$. The corresponding residual connections are incorporated to retain information and stability after each operation in $\texttt{Attn}^{(l)}$ and $\texttt{MLP}^{(l)}$.
L103: The architecture demonstrated above is based on a decoder-only autoregressive transformer model such as LLaMA^{2}^{2} 2 cite91†https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/tree/main/src/transformers/models/llama†github.com cite92†Touvron et al. (2023a) ; cite93†Touvron et al. (2023b) and Mistral^{3}^{3} 3 cite94†https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/tree/main/src/transformers/models/mistral†github.com cite95†Albert Q. Jiang et al. (2023) .
L104: ### 4.2 Proposed Method
L105: cite96†Image: Refer to caption Figure 1: An illustration of the proposed method – SABER. It utilizes a cross-layer residual connection in-between the outputs of layer $s$ and layer $e$. The connection originates from the normalized output of the layer $s$, adjusts its Euclidean Norm, and injects it with scaling factor $\lambda$. The outcome $v_{i}^{(s\rightarrow e)}$ is subsequently added to the output of the MLP and the standard residual connection at layer $e$.
L106: Note that the components outlined by dotted lines ($\cdots$) are essential to SABER.
L107: In this section, we introduce SABER, a novel approach that employs a cross-layer residual connection between the layer $s$ and $e$ ($s<e$) allowing it to circumvent safety mechanisms in LLMs. The impact of the proposed connection is regulated by a factor $\lambda$. The proposed approach SABER captures the normalized output activations ($\tilde{h}_{i}^{(s)}$) at an earlier layer $s$ and injects them at a later layer $e$, preserving the relative magnitude through norm-based scaling.
L108: Formally, SABER extends the standard architecture of the decoder-only autoregressive transformer based models (c.f. Section cite10†4.1 ) as follows:
L109:  |  | $\displaystyle h_{i}^{(l)}=h_{i}^{(l,\texttt{ mid})}+\texttt{MLP}^{(l)}(\tilde{h}_{i}^{(l,\texttt{ mid})})+\mathbbm{1}_{l=e}\cdot v_{i}^{(s\rightarrow e)}$  |
L110: 
L111: Here, the cross-layer residual connection is represented by $v_{i}^{(s\rightarrow e)}$ originates from layer $s$ and ends in layer $e$ (c.f. Figure cite97†1 ). It is defined as:
L112: 
L113:  |  | $\displaystyle v_{i}^{(s\rightarrow e)}=\tilde{h}_{i}^{(s)}\cdot\frac{\|h_{i}^{(e)}\|_{2}}{(\|\tilde{h}_{i}^{(s)}\|_{2}+\epsilon)}\cdot\lambda$  |
L114: where $\|\cdot\|_{2}$ represents the Euclidean norm along the embedding dimension, $\epsilon$^{4}^{4} 4 $\epsilon$ is set to $10^{-5}$. is added for numerical stability and $\lambda$ is a hyperparameter that controls the impact of the intervention. The normalized output $\tilde{h}_{i}^{(s)}$ (c.f. Equation cite98†1 ) is further normalized using the Euclidean norm prior to layer $e$.
L115: It helps retain the directional information from the source layer $s$, while scaling the magnitude of the influence based on the Euclidean norm of $h_{i}^{(e)}$ at layer $e$. Additionally, we prepend the phrase "Sure, here" to the beginning of the model’s response to further enhance jailbreaking effectiveness.
L116: We identify the optimal values for the parameters $(s^{*},e^{*},\lambda^{*})$ of SABER using a three-stage algorithm. In the first stage, we detect the layer boundaries for $s$ and $e$. The second stage focuses on finding the optimal scaling factor $\lambda^{*}$. Finally, the third stage is responsible for identifying the optimal pair $(s^{*},e^{*})$ within the range detected in the first stage. We will demonstrate each stage in detail.
L117: cite99†Image: Refer to caption Figure 2: An illustration of the average cosine dissimilarity between harmful and safe representation for all layers in the underlying model. The dissimilarity elevates notably in the middle layers with the most pronounced divergence occurring in the middle-to-late layers across all models. Algorithm 1 Finding Layer Boundaries

L120: Output: The layer boundaries $(s^{\prime},e^{\prime})$

L144: #### 4.2.1 Detection of Layer Boundaries
L145: The goal of the first stage is to identify the layer boundaries that may play a key role in safety mechanisms. We examine how internal representations of inputs ($x$) diverge across the layers. The hidden states of the last input token, $h_{\text{x}}^{(l)}$, from each layer $l$ are used to compute the pairwise cosine dissimilarity between harmful and safe inputs.
L146: Our analysis reveals that the dissimilarity between harmful and safe inputs progressively rises mostly in the middle layers and reaches the peak at middle-to-late layers (c.f. Figure cite100†2 ). It indicates that safety mechanisms are most prevalent in middle-to-late regions. We compute the first-order differences in the average cosine dissimilarity between harmful and safe representations across layers to identify the boundaries where these differences are most pronounced.
L147: Specifically, we evaluate the change in cosine distance between successive layers with a threshold, $\tau$^{5}^{5} 5 The value of $\tau$ is set to $0.04$ to select the boundary indices i.e. $(s^{\prime},e^{\prime})$. The full procedure is detailed in Algorithm cite101†1 .
L148: #### 4.2.2 Finding the Optimal Scaling Factor

L182: Next, we find the optimal scaling factor, denoted as $\lambda^{*}$ that maximizes the impact while preserving general language modeling capabilities. To ensure the balance, we employ Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence to quantify the discrepancy between output distributions with and without SABER (c.f. Algorithm cite102†2 ). The algorithm iterates over a predefined set of candidate $\lambda$ values, $\Lambda$.
L183: For each value of $\lambda$, we compute the average distributional difference between the output of the original model, $\mathcal{M}_{\theta}$ and the modified model, $\mathcal{M}_{\theta,s,e}$. Here, $\pi^{x}_{\text{orig}}$ and $\pi^{x}_{s,e,\lambda}$ represents the probability distribution over the final token of $x$ from $\mathcal{M}_{\theta}$ and $\mathcal{M}_{\theta,s,e}$, respectively.
L184: Note that $\mathcal{M}_{\theta,s,e}$ is modified with a residual connection from layer $s$ to layer $e$ scaled by a factor of $\lambda$. For each instance in $\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}^{\text{ val}}$, a pair of layer $(s,e)$ is randomly selected within valid boundaries i.e. $(s^{\prime},e^{\prime})$ to incorporate the residual connection.
L185: The algorithm accumulates the average KL divergence for each $\lambda$ over $\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}^{\text{ val}}$ but retains only those values in $\lambda^{*}_{list}$ if the divergence remains below a threshold of $\psi$^{6}^{6} 6 The value of $\psi$ is set to $0.05$. It ensures minimal impact of SABER on the model’s general performance for benign inputs while maximizing the impact on harmful prompts. Finally, it returns the maximum value from $\lambda^{*}_{list}$.

L216: end for
L217: #### 4.2.3 Identification of the Optimal Pair
L218: Now, we identify the pair of optimal layers, denoted as $(s^{*},e^{*})$ within the range defined by $(s^{\prime},e^{\prime})$ (c.f. Algorithm cite103†3 ). It considers all possible pairs of layers $(i,j)$ where $i<j$ and an altered model $\mathcal{M}_{\theta,i,j}$ with a residual connection from layer $i$ to layer $j$.
L219: The altered model $\mathcal{M}_{\theta,i,j}$ is evaluated on the $\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}}^{\text{val}}$ validation set, yielding a success rate using the HarmBench metric defined in Section cite19†5.4 . Finally, the pair $(i,j)$ with the highest success rate is returned as the optimal configuration $(s^{*},e^{*})$. We evaluate all possible pairs within the identified boundaries to pinpoint the optimal pair $(s^{*},e^{*})$ that yields highest success rate on $\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}}^{\text{ val}}$.
L220: Additional information regarding the optimal value for each of the parameters are given in Appendix cite37†A.3 .
L221: ## 5 Experimental Setup
L222: 
L223: ### 5.1 Models
L224: 
L225: We integrate SABER with four alternative models: (i) Llama-2-7b-chat^{7}^{7} 7 cite104†https://huggingface.co/meta-llama†huggingface.co (L2-7BCh) (ii) Llama-2-13b-chat (L2-13BCh) (iii) Vicuna-7b-v1.5^{8}^{8} 8 cite105†https://huggingface.co/lmsys†huggingface.co (V-7B) and (iv) Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2^{9}^{9} 9 cite106†https://huggingface.co/mistralai†huggingface.co (M-7BInst).
L226: ### 5.2 Benchmark Datasets
L227: We benchmark SABER against the baselines (c.f. Section cite18†5.3 ) and its architectural variants (c.f. Section cite20†5.5 ) on $\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}}^{\text{ test}}$ and $\mathcal{D}_{\text{harm}}^{\text{ val}}$ of the HarmBench dataset, respectively . To further validate the effectiveness of SABER under more stringent scenario, we leverage $520$ instances from AdvBench cite107†Biarese (2022) and $100$ instances from JailbreakBench (JbBench) cite108†Chao et al. (2024) .
L228: Moreover, we report whether SABER negatively affects the general capabilities of the models or not through assessing the models (c.f. Section cite16†5.1 ) based on the coherence of generated outputs and their performance in reasoning tasks, both with and without SABER on widely recognized benchmarks: MMLU cite109†Hendrycks et al. (2020) , TinyHellaSwag cite110†Zellers et al. (2019) , ARC cite111†Clark et al. (2018) , WinoGrande cite112†Sakaguchi et al. (2021) and TruthfulQA cite113†Lin et al. (2021) .
L229: Additional information on the evaluation prompts is presented in Appendix cite42†B .
L230: ### 5.3 Baseline
L231: We use the following baselines against SABER: (i) GCG cite70†Zou et al. (2023b) , (ii) GCG-M, (iii) GCG-T, (iv) AutoPrompt cite114†Shin et al. (2020) , (v) PAIR cite115†Chao et al. (2023) and (vii) AutoDAN cite116†Liu et al. (2023) . GCG is a token-level method that optimizes an adversarial suffix to increase the likelihood of an inappropriate target string.
L232: It has two variants: (i) GCG-M that optimizes a single adversarial suffix to be appended with multiple user prompts, each targeting a different target string; and (ii) GCG-T that builds upon GCG-M by simultaneously optimizing the adversarial suffix across multiple training models. AutoPrompt is similar to GCG, but it uses a different strategy for selection of candidate prompts. PAIR opts for iterative prompting strategy to explore and adaptively obtain harmful responses.

L36: # Robust Vision-Language Models via Tensor Decomposition: A Defense Against Adversarial Attacks
L37: 
L38: Het Patel    Muzammil Allie    Qian Zhang    Jia Chen    Evangelos E. Papalexakis Affiliation: University of California, Riverside Affiliation: {hpate061, malli007, qzhang, jiac, epapalex}@ucr.edu
L39: ###### Abstract
L40: Vision language models (VLMs) excel in multimodal understanding but are prone to adversarial attacks. Existing defenses often demand costly retraining or significant architecture changes. We introduce a lightweight defense using tensor decomposition suitable for any pre-trained VLM, requiring no retraining. By decomposing and reconstructing vision encoder representations, it filters adversarial noise while preserving meaning. Experiments with CLIP on COCO and Flickr30K show improved robustness.
L41: On Flickr30K, it restores 12.3% performance lost to attacks, raising Recall@1 accuracy from 7.5% to 19.8%. On COCO, it recovers 8.1% performance, improving accuracy from 3.8% to 11.9%. Analysis shows Tensor Train decomposition with low rank (8-32) and low residual strength ($\alpha=0.1-0.2$) is optimal. This method is a practical, plug-and-play solution with minimal overhead for existing VLMs.
L42: ## 1 Introduction
L43: Vision language models (VLMs) such as CLIP[cite24†15 ] have revolutionized multimodal understanding by learning joint embeddings of images and text, enabling applications like image retrieval[cite25†8 ], zero-shot classification[cite26†14 ], and visual question answering[cite27†21 ]. However, VLMs remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks[cite28†11 , cite29†19 ], where imperceptible perturbations dramatically degrade performance. Ensuring robustness is essential as these models deploy in critical applications.
L44: Traditional defenses like adversarial training[cite30†10 ], input preprocessing[cite31†20 ], and architectural modifications[cite32†13 ] have significant limitations: adversarial training requires expensive retraining on large datasets, while architectural changes demand substantial redevelopment effort. For large pre-trained VLMs, these solutions are often impractical due to computational constraints or unavailable training data.
L45: We propose a novel tensor decomposition defense applicable to any pretrained VLM without retraining or modification. Leveraging the fact that adversarial perturbations introduce high-frequency noise in feature representations[cite33†9 ], we decompose and reconstruct intermediate representations using low-rank tensor approximations to filter perturbations while preserving semantic content.
L46: Our contributions include: (1) a lightweight tensor decomposition defense requiring no retraining, (2) comprehensive parameter analysis, (3) empirical robustness improvements on COCO and Flickr30K, and (4) publicly available code at cite34†GitHub Link†github.com .
L47: ## 2 Related Work
L48: 
L49: Defensive Tensorization [cite35†2 ] applies Tucker decomposition to express CNN weight tensors in lower-dimensional latent spaces, introducing tensor dropout to stochastically reduce tensor ranks and prevent adversarial exploitation of fixed-weight structures.
L50: Input-level defenses include SmoothVLM[cite36†16 ], which uses random pixel perturbations with majority voting(achieving 95% attack reduction), and TensorSHIELD[cite37†4 ], which filters adversarial noise via low-rank tensor decompositions. FARE[cite38†17 ] utilizes unsupervised alignment between perturbed and original images for consistent outputs withouit labeled data.

L61: Double Visual Defense[cite29†19 ] improves the robustness using a two-stage adversarial training process: extensive pretraining to boost zero-shot capabilities and attack resistance, followed by fine-tuning on downstream tasks with adversarially perturbed inputs.
L62: Current approaches have notable limitations: Defensive Tensorization factorizes weight matrices without considering input variations, SmoothVLM requires multiple forward passes per query, TensorSHIELD lacks dynamic adaptation, and FARE and Double Visual Defense demand substantial computational resources and frequent dataset updates against evolving attacks.
L63: ## 3 Methodology
L64: 
L65: We present a defense mechanism against adversarial attacks on a vision-language model utilizing tensor decomposition techniques[cite42†6 , cite43†1 , cite44†3 ], including CP/PARAFAC[cite45†5 ], Tucker[cite46†18 ], and Tensor-Train Decomposition[cite47†12 ]. Our approach works by applying low-rank tensor decompositions to the internal representation of the CLIP model.
L66: ### 3.1 Problem Formulation
L67: 
L68: We consider a pre-trained VLM that maps images and text to a joint embedding space. For an image-text pair $(I,T)$, the model produces embeddings $f_{I}(I)$ and $f_{T}(T)$. During inference, the similarity between these embeddings is computed as:
L69: 
L70:  | $$s(I,T)=\langle f_{I}(I),f_{T}(T)\rangle$$  |  | (1)
L71: 
L72: where $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ denotes the cosine similarity.
L73: 
L74: An adversarial attack aims to find a perturbed image $I_{adv}$ such that:
L75:  | $$I_{adv}=I+\delta,\text{ where }\|\delta\|_{\infty}\leq\epsilon$$  |  | (2)
L76: 
L77: The perturbation $\delta$ is designed to minimize the similarity between the perturbed image and its corresponding text description:
L78: 
L79:  | $$\min_{\delta}s(I+\delta,T)\text{ subject to }\|\delta\|_{\infty}\leq\epsilon$$  |  | (3)
L80: 
L81: Our goal is to defend against such attacks by restoring the correct cross-modal alignment in the presence of adversarial perturbations.
L82: ### 3.2 Adversarial Attack Framework
L83: 
L84: We use a white-box approach known as Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) specifically on CLIP models. Given an image-text $(x,t)$ pairs, the attack minimizes the cosine similarity between their embeddings:
L85: 
L86:  | $$L_{adv}(x_{adv},t)=-\frac{f_{I}(x_{adv})\cdot f_{T}(t)}{||f_{I}(x_{adv})||\cdot||f_{T}(t)||}$$  |
L87: 
L88: where $f_{I}$ and $f_{T}$ are the image and text encoders. The adversarial example $x_{adv}$ is generated through iterative updates:
L89:  | $$x_{adv}^{i+1}=\Pi_{\epsilon}(x_{adv}^{i}+\alpha\cdot\text{sign}(\nabla_{x}L_{adv}(x_{adv}^{i},t)))$$  |
L90: with perturbation budget $\epsilon=8/255$, step size $\alpha=6/255$, and $\Pi_{\epsilon}$ projected onto the $\ell_{\infty}$ ball around the original image. The $\ell_{\infty}$-ball constraint ensures that no pixel in the adversarial image differs from the corresponding pixel in the original image by more than $\epsilon$, maintaining perceptual similarity while allowing effective attacks (Fig. cite48†1 ).
L91: ### 3.3 Tensor Decomposition Defense
L92: 
L93: Our defense mechanism simplifies CLIP vision encoder representations through three components:
L94: 
L95:   1. 1.
L96: 
L97: Forward Hook Mechanism: Intercepts tensors at specific layers (final_norm, attention, MLP outputs).
L98: 
L99:   2. 2.
L100: 
L101: Tensor Decomposition: Applies one of three methods to tensor $T$:
L102: 
L103:      * •
L104: 
L105: CP: $T\approx\sum_{r=1}^{R}a_{r}\circ b_{r}\circ c_{r}$ (rank-1 tensor sums)
L106: 
L107:      * •
L108: 
L109: Tucker: $T\approx\mathcal{G}\times_{1}A\times_{2}B\times_{3}C$ (core tensor + factors)
L110:      * •
L111: 
L112: TT: $T[i_{1},\ldots,i_{d}]\approx G_{1}[i_{1}]\cdots G_{d}[i_{d}]$ (3D core products)
L113: 
L114:   3. 3.
L115: 
L116: Residual Connection: $T_{\text{final}}=\alpha\cdot T+(1-\alpha)\cdot\hat{T}$, where $\alpha$ controls defense strength.
L117: ## 4 Experimental Setup
L118: 
L119: We used CLIP (ViT-B/32) on MS-COCO and Flickr30K datasets, evaluating 1,000 pairs for parameter analysis and 3,000 for comprehensive evaluation. Attacks used PGD with $\ell_{\infty}$ constraint: $\epsilon=8/255$, step size $\alpha=6/255$, and 10 steps, creating imperceptible perturbations that significantly degrade performance (Fig. cite48†1 ).
L120: Our tensor decomposition defense, implemented with PyTorch and TensorLy[cite49†7 ], uses forward hooks with random initialization, 50 iterations, and $10^{-4}$ tolerance. We evaluated five key factors:
L121: 
L122:   1. 1.
L123: 
L124: Decomposition Method: CP, Tucker, and Tensor Train effectiveness
L125: 
L126:   2. 2.
L127: 
L128: Target Layer: Final norm, attention output, and MLP layers
L129: 
L130:   3. 3.
L131: 
L132: Rank Parameter: Values from 16-256 exploring capacity vs. noise filtering
L133: 
L134:   4. 4.
L135: Residual Strength: Weight $\alpha$ (0.1-0.9) balancing original and reconstructed features
L136: 
L137:   5. 5.
L138: 
L139: Multi-layer Configuration: Single layer up to all 12 transformer layers
L140: ## 5 Results and Analysis
L141: 
L142: ### 5.1 Parameter Sensitivity Analysis
L143: #### 5.1.1 Effect of $\alpha$ Value
L144: 
L145: cite50†Image: Refer to caption Figure 2: Performance comparison across different $\alpha$ values using Tensor Train decomposition (rank=32) on the final normalization layer. Lower $\alpha$ values provide better defense against adversarial attacks.
L146: The effectiveness of tensor decomposition is greatly affected by the residual connection strength parameter $\alpha$, which balances the original and decomposed forms. As seen in cite51†2 , there is an inverse relationship between $\alpha$ values and model robustness in the MS-COCO and Flickr30K datasets. Performance peaks at lower $\alpha$ values (0.1-0.3) and declines as $\alpha$ increases. For Flickr30K, the best Recall@1 is 10.6% at $\alpha=0.3$, and for MS-COCO, it is 6.2% at $\alpha=0.1$.
L147: The downward trend with increasing $\alpha$ supports that adversarial perturbations, as high-frequency components, are effectively filtered by tensor decomposition.
L148: #### 5.1.2 Decomposition Rank
L149: 
L150: cite52†Image: Refer to caption Figure 3: Performance comparison across different rank values using Tensor Train decomposition ($\alpha=0.2$) on the final normalization layer, lower rank values (8-32) provide greater defense against adversarial attacks, while performance degrades significantly at higher ranks.
L151: The decomposition rank is a critical parameter that determines the representational capacity of the tensor decomposition. Figure cite53†3 illustrates the effect of varying rank values on adversarial defense performance in the MS-COCO and Flickr30K datasets, with $\alpha$ fixed at 0.2 and applied to the final normalization layer.
L152: Our results reveal an intriguing pattern: lower rank values (8-32) consistently achieve the highest performance on both datasets, with Recall@1 scores of 10.7% for Flickr30k and 6.3-6.4% for MS-COCO. Performance remains relatively stable across the 8-96 rank range, with only a modest decline, but drops significantly as rank increases beyond 96. At the highest tested ranks (256-512), performance decreases dramatically to 7.6% and 4.5% for Flickr30k and MS-COCO, respectively.
L153: These findings also validate our assumption that adversarial perturbations manifest themselves primarily as high-frequency components in the feature space. Lower-rank decompositions effectively filter out these perturbations while preserving the essential semantic structure required for cross-modal understanding. As rank increases, the decomposition retains more of the original feature structure, including adversarial noise, reducing the effectiveness of the defense.
L154: #### 5.1.3 Decomposition Method
L155: 
L156: cite54†Image: Refer to caption Figure 4: Tensor decomposition methods (CP, Tucker, TT) applied to normalization layers of the last five transformer blocks. All methods substantially improve over adversarial baselines of 3.8% (MS-COCO) and 7.5% (Flickr30k), with TT decomposition achieving best performance: 19.8% (Flickr30k) and 11.9% (MS-COCO).
L157: We evaluated three tensor decomposition methods (CP, Tucker, TT) applied to normalization layers of the last five transformer blocks. Figure cite55†4 shows that TT consistently outperforms others: on Flickr30k, TT achieves 19.8% vs Tucker’s 15.4% and CP’s 10.0%; on MS-COCO, TT reaches 11.9% vs Tucker’s 11.2% and CP’s 7.3%. This represents 12.3 and 8.1 percentage point recoveries, respectively, from adversarial baselines.
L158: TT’s superiority stems from decomposing tensors into three-dimensional core sequences that preserve structural information better than CP’s rank-one components, effectively filtering adversarial perturbations while retaining semantic content. Tucker’s core tensor structure effectively captures higher-order interactions, whereas CP’s simpler rank-one approximation proves insufficient for optimal adversarial filtering.
L159: #### 5.1.4 Target Layer
L160: 
L161: cite56†Image: Refer to caption Figure 5: Performance comparison of TT decomposition ($\alpha=0.2$ rank=32) applied to different components and configurations. Single-layer defense is applied to the final normalization, attention output, and MLP layers, compared against multi-layer implementations on the last two and last five transformer block normalization layers.
L162: Figure cite57†5 illustrates the effectiveness of Tensor Train decomposition on various CLIP vision encoder components. The impact differs by component, with the final normalization layer offering the best defense in single layers. Extending to multiple layers improves results, with optimal outcomes from addressing the normalization layers of the last five blocks across all methods and datasets.
L163: #### 5.1.5 Computational Efficiency

This advantage extends to multilayer configurations, with 5-layer TT presenting a reasonable 3.93x overhead given its strong defensive capabilities, offering a tunable security-performance trade-off.
L174: ## 6 Conclusion
L175: 
L176: We presented a lightweight tensor decomposition defense that significantly improves VLM robustness against adversarial attacks without retraining or architectural modifications. Comprehensive experiments on COCO and Flickr30k using CLIP demonstrated effective adversarial filtering while preserving semantic content.
L177: Key findings: (1) Tensor Train decomposition outperformed CP and Tucker methods, recovering up to 12.3% performance with minimal computational overhead; (2) lower ranks (8-32) and residual strength ($\alpha=0.1-0.3$) provided optimal defense by filtering high-frequency adversarial components; (3) normalization layer targeting and multi-layer configurations (last five blocks) yielded strongest results; (4) TT decomposition achieved favorable efficiency with only 22% overhead while maintaining 82% throughput.
L178: This plug-and-play approach offers practical advantages over methods requiring extensive retraining. Future work will explore adaptive rank selection and effectiveness in other VLM architectures and attack types.
L179: ## 7 Limitations
L180: Although our tensor decomposition defense demonstrates promising results, several limitations must be acknowledged. First, our exploration was limited in time and resources, preventing exhaustive testing of all decomposition methods, rank values, and $\alpha$ parameters, and there might be better configurations outside our tested space. Second, we utilized three classical techniques (CP, Tucker, and TT), but advanced methods, such as Hierarchical Tucker or Block-Term Decomposition, could be more effective.
L181: Our tests focused on the CLIP model and PGD attacks; however, the effectiveness of this approach on other architectures or advanced attacks remains untested. Although retraining is not necessary, our approach adds inference-time computation that may hinder some real-time applications, especially with multi-layer configurations.
